statement: In couples in which one partner had PTSD (two small uncontrolled studies sharing an author: 6 White heterosexual couples in which both partners took MDMA twice within a condensed course of cognitive-behavioral conjoint therapy, and 8 US veteran couples in which only the veteran took MDMA twice within an eight-session brief version), clinician-rated PTSD symptoms fell after treatment (CAPS-5, scale 0 to 80: from about 41 to 19 in the first study, with 5 of 6 patients no longer meeting PTSD criteria; a mean fall of 16 points from 39 in the second, with 3 of 8 no longer meeting criteria and a rebound of about 6 points by 6 months), and both partners' relationship satisfaction rose (in the second study it partly fell back, and one partner's worsened). All couples completed treatment and no serious adverse event was reported. Neither study had a comparison group, the conjoint therapy improves PTSD without MDMA, and in the veteran study loss of diagnosis was about as frequent as with the brief therapy alone in an earlier trial in the same population, so whether MDMA adds anything is not known. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.
plain: In two small studies, couples in which one partner had PTSD had couples therapy that included MDMA sessions. PTSD and relationship scores improved, and no one had a serious side effect. But neither study had a group without MDMA, and this couples therapy also helps without it, so we do not know if MDMA added anything.
population: Couples (married or committed, almost all heterosexual) in which one partner had chronic PTSD on the CAPS-5 and the other did not; severe relationship aggression or intimate partner violence and current substance use disorders excluded; psychiatric medicines stopped for the PTSD partner (and, in the first study, both partners)
exposure: Two MDMA sessions within cognitive-behavioral conjoint therapy for PTSD: both partners dosed within the full 15-session protocol condensed into 7 weeks (first study), or only the partner with PTSD dosed within an 8-session brief protocol with integration sessions drawing on couple therapy (second study)
comparator: None: change from baseline in each study
outcome: CAPS-5 PTSD severity and diagnosis; relationship satisfaction (Couples Satisfaction Index) and other relational measures; adverse events; up to 6 months
magnitude: First study (6 couples; model-estimated means): CAPS-5 41.42 (SD 5.76) before treatment, 19.37 (13.71) after and 15.52 (15.22) at 6 months (within-group d 2.10 and 2.25); registry: CAPS-5 change −25.7 (SD 13.89); Couples Satisfaction Index, patients 105.37 to 127.00 (d 0.82) and partners 98.10 to 125.34 (d 0.64) after treatment. Second study (8 veteran couples): CAPS-5 39.13 (10.56) at baseline, mean fall 16.1 (SD 11.4) during treatment, response 5 of 8, loss of diagnosis 3 of 8, remission 2 of 8, rebound 6.3 points by 6 months; satisfaction d 1.83 (veterans) and 1.29 (partners) during treatment, rebound d −0.68 and −0.47; reliable improvement in 10 of 16 people and reliable deterioration in 1 partner.

evidence.locator: 2. Results › 2.1 PTSD and patient comorbid outcomes, 1st paragraph; Tables 2 and 3
evidence.extracted: Six couples: CAPS-5 41.42 (5.76) before treatment, 19.37 (13.71) after, 17.43 (17.14) at 3 months and 15.52 (15.22) at 6 months (estimated means); B = −4.64, P < .001; within-group d 2.10, 1.88 and 2.25; all but one patient had a sustained remission of the clinician-assessed PTSD diagnosis.

evidence.locator: 2. Results › 2.2 Intimate relationship outcomes, 1st paragraph; Tables 2 and 3
evidence.extracted: Couples Satisfaction Index: patients 105.37 (13.39) to 127.00 after treatment and 130.78 at 6 months, B = 4.55, P < .05, d 0.82 to 1.22; partners 98.10 (50.81) to 125.34 and 130.10, B = 5.73, P < .05, d 0.64 to 0.80; one patient satisfied at baseline was dissatisfied afterwards.
All six couples completed the protocol and there were no serious adverse events; the authors state that the lack of randomization or a control condition severely limits the conclusions.

evidence.locator: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02876172 (API v2) › Results › Outcome Measures; Adverse Events
evidence.extracted: Posted results: CAPS-5 at the primary endpoint 16.3 (13.71), change −25.7 (13.89), n = 6; all 6 patients and all 6 partners had at least one non-serious adverse event up to 2 months after the last MDMA session; no serious events or deaths.

evidence.locator: Results › Outcomes › Trauma-Related Outcomes and Relationship Quality Outcomes, 1st paragraphs; Tables 1 and 2
evidence.extracted: Same six couples: the patient's posttraumatic growth rose as rated by patients (B = 7.30) and partners (B = 7.63), both P < 0.001; perceived support and social intimacy rose for both partners (intimacy B = 4.12 and 3.10); relationship depth did not change; the printed SORTS means duplicate another measure's values (card reporting issue).

evidence.locator: RESULTS › PTSD symptom severity, 1st paragraph; Fig. 3 note
evidence.extracted: Eight veterans: CAPS-5 39.13 (10.56) at baseline; during treatment d = −1.25, mean fall 16.1 points (SD 11.4; range 3 to 34); response 5 of 8, loss of diagnosis 3 of 8, remission 2 of 8; rebound during follow-up of 6.3 points (d = 0.29).

Relationship satisfaction (CSI-32): d = 1.83 for veterans and 1.29 for partners during treatment, mean rise 27.9 (31.8) and 19.8 (23.1); rebound d = −0.68 and −0.47 during follow-up; reliable improvement in 10 of 16, reliable deterioration in 1 partner.

The authors report that CBCT without MDMA has shown large reductions in PTSD symptoms (gs 1.28 to 1.71, citing Monson et al., 2024) and that their eight-session brief CBCT, without MDMA, reduced PTSD in veterans (ds 1.05 to 1.12; Morland et al., 2022) with smaller relationship gains; these figures are second-hand.

Loss of diagnosis (37.5%) and remission (25%) were lower than in the phase 3 MDMA trials and, the authors say, closer to brief CBCT without MDMA in the same population; the open-label design, small sample and lack of a comparison condition preclude causal inference.

evidence.locator: RESULTS › Safety › AEs and Medication management, 1st paragraphs; RESULTS › Feasibility and acceptability
evidence.extracted: All couples completed every session; no serious adverse events; every veteran had at least one treatment-emergent adverse event; one veteran's second MDMA session was rescheduled after a cocaine-positive urine test.

risk_of_bias.note: Critical: no comparison; base therapy effective without MDMA.

grade.reasoning: Two uncontrolled studies (14 couples in all), non-randomized: start low. Risk of bias two levels (ROBINS-I critical in both): no comparison group, and the base therapy is an established treatment that improves PTSD on its own, so MDMA's contribution cannot be separated from the therapy, time or expectation; outcomes unblinded. Imprecision one level: 6 and 8 couples. Inconsistency not rated down: both studies improved, though the second rebounded. Status 'replicated by the same team' because the studies share an author (Anne C. Wagner) and a related protocol; the second sample is independent. The relation is 'insufficient evidence' about any added effect of MDMA.
